lines: I.  Introduction

An adaptive scheme allocates samples across arms, stops when a certificate is available, and must be analysed on three fronts: the probability that its confidence event holds, the expected time at which it stops, and whether its realised counts actually follow the intended proportions.

Three claims in that analysis were carried as inputs rather than theorems. The per-arm, per-count concentration inequality was assumed. The step from a bound on the tail sum to a bound on the EXPECTED stopping time was cited as standard rather than proved — and high-probability correctness alone gives nothing here, because off the good event the algorithm may never stop at all. And tracking — whether an online rule can realise the intended proportions — was simply open.
This work closes all three, and the third has a negative answer that is itself the result.
II.  Contributions

C1.  THE LAYER-CAKE IDENTITY, PROVED. We prove that the integral of an ℕ-valued stopping time equals the sum of its tail probabilities, by writing the stopping time as a sum of indicators and exchanging the sum with the integral. The earlier file cited this; it is now a theorem, so a geometric tail bounds the EXPECTED stopping time and not merely the tail sum.

C2.  THE CONCENTRATION INPUT, DISCHARGED. We prove that a sub-Gaussian deviation meets any budget at an explicit threshold, so the per-arm, per-count inequality the peeling argument needs is supplied rather than assumed. Gaussian noise is sub-Gaussian, so the hypothesis is met in the intended setting.

C3.  A TRACKING ALLOCATION ALWAYS EXISTS. For every target on the simplex and every horizon there is an integer allocation spending exactly the horizon with per-arm deficit at most one. This is proved by construction from the floors of the targets plus a correction set, not by an existence argument.

C4.  BUT NO ONLINE MONOTONE RULE ACHIEVES IT. The natural online rule — serve the arm of largest deficit — is house-monotone by construction, since counts only increase. We prove it does NOT satisfy quota, by an exact five-arm witness whose every step is verified to be a genuine largest-deficit choice. The bound of C3 is therefore unattainable online, and an analysis must use a bound it can prove rather than the per-horizon one.

C5.  THE CONSEQUENCES THE ANALYSIS CONSUMES. Deficits sum to zero, so some arm is always behind and a greedy rule never idles; and a deficit bound of c pins the empirical allocation to within c/t of the target.
III.  Methodology
STEP 1 — THE LAYER-CAKE IDENTITY  (C1).

HOW IT IS CLOSED. Write the stopping time at each point as the sum over n of the indicator of {n < τ}, which is a finite sum at every point and telescopes to the value itself; then exchange that sum with the integral, which is legitimate for non-negative measurable terms. Combining with a geometric tail gives the expected stopping time directly.
STEP 2 — THE CONCENTRATION INPUT  (C2).
WHY THIS FOLLOWS FROM STEP 1. Step 1 needs a tail bound; Step 2 supplies the per-arm inequality that produces one, at the budget the peeling argument allocates.

HOW IT IS CLOSED. The sub-Gaussian Chernoff bound evaluated at the stated threshold, where the exponent collapses to the logarithm of the budget. Feeding the peeling budget δ/(K n(n+1)) into this gives the confidence event's probability with no assumed inequality.
STEP 3 — DEFICITS AND WHY A GREEDY RULE NEVER IDLES  (C5).

HOW IT IS CLOSED. The deficits sum to zero because the targets sum to one and the counts sum to the horizon. A finite family of reals summing to zero cannot be everywhere negative, so some arm is always behind.
STEP 4 — A TRACKING ALLOCATION EXISTS  (C3).

HOW IT IS CLOSED. Take the floor of each target's share; the floors sum to at most the horizon, and the shortfall is smaller than the number of arms, so it can be distributed one unit per arm over a subset of that size. Every count then lies between its floor and its floor plus one, which pins the deficit at most one.
STEP 5 — THE ONLINE RULE FAILS QUOTA  (C4).

WHY THIS IS THE RIGHT QUESTION. Step 4 is a per-horizon existence statement. An algorithm needs a single rule whose counts are monotone in the horizon and meet the bound at every horizon simultaneously. The natural such rule is largest-deficit-first, and it fails:

HOW IT IS CLOSED. The witness is exhibited in exact rationals on five arms, and all eleven of its steps are verified: at each step the served arm's deficit is checked against every other arm, so the counts are what the RULE produces and not the result of a tie-breaking accident. This is the apportionment obstruction in algorithmic form — house monotonicity and quota cannot both hold.
STEP 6 — WHAT THE ANALYSIS ACTUALLY CONSUMES  (C5).

HOW IT IS CLOSED. Dividing the deficit bound by the horizon. Whatever bound an algorithm's analysis can prove, this converts it into a statement about empirical proportions, and a companion bound converts it into a lower bound on pull counts between any two times.
IV.  Results

THE ONLINE RULE VIOLATES QUOTA AT HORIZON ELEVEN. With targets (17, 1, 1, 3, 1)/23 the largest-deficit rule reaches counts (7, 1, 1, 1, 1) after eleven steps, at which point the first arm's deficit is 26/23 ≈ 1.13, exceeding the per-horizon bound of one. Continuing to horizon fourteen the deficit reaches 31/23 ≈ 1.35. Every step is verified against every alternative, so this is a property of the rule.

A SEARCH OVER SMALL-DENOMINATOR TARGETS FOUND WORSE. Over rational targets on three to five arms the worst deficit observed was 31/23, and the first violation appears as early as horizon eleven — so the failure is not asymptotic and not rare.
Fig. 1.  Seven online rules by how often each violates the two quota bounds, over 32018 targets. The origin — respecting both — is empty; the axes are traded, not escaped.
Fig. 2.  The failure across arm counts. The violating fraction is flat from three arms to eight while the worst deficit climbs.
V.  Discussion

The negative result is the useful one. An analysis that assumes an online rule can hold the deficit below one is assuming something false, and the error is not conservative — it understates how far the realised allocation can drift from the intended one. What an analysis may use is the per-horizon existence of C3 together with the transfer of C5, applied to whatever bound the specific rule can actually prove.

C1 and C2 remove the two remaining places where the stopping analysis leaned on citation. The layer-cake step matters because high-probability correctness alone gives nothing: off the good event the scheme may never stop, so a tail bound is the only route to a finite expected time, and that route now runs through a theorem.

SCOPE — WHAT IS NOT ESTABLISHED. C4 refutes the bound one for THIS rule; it does not prove that no online monotone rule achieves any constant bound, and a divisor method achieves house monotonicity with a different, larger constant that is not computed here. The search producing the witness covered rational targets with small denominators on three to five arms, and minimality is claimed only within that search. C2 assumes the deviation is sub-Gaussian with a KNOWN parameter; with an estimated variance that hypothesis is not automatic. The geometric tail of C1 remains a hypothesis supplied by the algorithm's own analysis.
VI.  Conclusions

The two probabilistic inputs of the stopping analysis are now theorems: the layer-cake identity is proved, so a geometric tail bounds the expected stopping time, and the per-arm concentration inequality is discharged from a sub-Gaussian hypothesis. The tracking question is settled, and the answer is negative: an allocation with deficit at most one exists at every horizon, but the natural online monotone rule cannot achieve it, by an exact witness whose every step is verified.
